title: Fitting a letterbox draught seal
subtitle: Fit a brush-pile or flap-type draught seal inside a letterbox plate to stop cold air passing through the door
excerpt: How to fit a draught seal inside an existing letterbox opening. Covers removing the old plate, fitting a brush-pile seal or a hinged-flap type, and refitting the plate.
sourceNotes: Collins Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). Reader's Digest Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). UK Energy Saving Trust guidance on draught-proofing (open access).

glossaryTerms.definition: A frame fitted behind a letterbox plate that carries two rows of dense nylon brush pile. Letters and leaflets push through the brush. The brush closes against the opposing pile row, blocking cold air, wind, and rain from passing through the slot.

content.text: An unsealed letterbox is one of the biggest sources of draught in an external door. A
fits inside the existing letterbox opening, behind the external plate. The job is remove, fit, and refix. Tools needed are a screwdriver and the new seal unit.

Before buying, measure the letterbox opening width and depth. Most standard letterboxes in the UK are 254 mm (10 inches) wide with a slot depth of 35-38 mm. The brush seal frame must fit snugly within the opening. Brush seals are available in standard sizes to fit most letterboxes; if yours is non-standard, measure and order the closest smaller size (a slightly smaller frame still seals effectively and is better than one that does not fit).

Open the door and look at the inner face. The letterbox plate is usually secured by two long bolts passing through the door from the outer plate. Undo the inner retaining nuts with a screwdriver or pliers. The outer plate and the inner flap or tidy plate will come away together. Note how the existing fixings work before removing them.

Insert the brush-seal frame from the inside of the door into the letterbox opening. Most frames clip or slide into place and do not need separate fixing. The two brush-pile rows should sit across the full width of the slot. Check that the brushes meet in the middle and that a piece of card slipped through meets resistance from both sides. Refit the outer plate and inner tidy plate, tightening the bolts just enough to hold everything firm without bowing the door face.

Some letterboxes are sealed instead with an internal hinged tidy plate that closes flat against the door face under its own weight. This gives a stronger draught seal but letters that bend as they come through can push the flap open. The fixing method is the same: the hinged plate is screwed or bolted to the inner door face on the fixing bolts from the outer plate.

attrs.symptom: The brush seal works loose and drops into the letterbox after a few weeks
attrs.cause: The frame was not clipped fully into the opening, or the opening is slightly wider than the frame.
attrs.fix: Remove and apply a bead of silicone sealant around the perimeter of the frame before refitting; this holds it in place and improves the seal.

attrs.symptom: Mail catches on the brush and tears
attrs.cause: Brush pile too dense or too long for the slot depth.
attrs.fix: Trim the brush pile slightly with scissors, or switch to a shorter-pile brush seal.
